item.title: An Exploration of Attacks on AI Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.12524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As autonomous AI agents become more integrated into sensitive domains, it is crucial that single and multi-agent AI systems are secured. This paper investigates how prompt injection attacks can exploit both direct user inputs and inter?agent communication to leak sensitive information and trigger cross-agent infections. While our tests mostly highlight key vulnerabilities in single-agent systems, we also extend these attacks to multi-agent frameworks, investigating how weaknesses can propagate across agents. Our findings emphasize the need for more robust defenses as AI agents become more commonly embedded in real-world workflows.
item.dc:creator: Cathleen Qiao, Layah Vigneaud, Chloe Brandon, Max Cabilangan, Xiyuan Cao, Isaac Khabra, Reva Mahajan, Lena Nguyen, Kyle Pak, Anagh Pandya, Roshni Dave, Peiran Wang

item.title: SoK: Privacy-Preserving Order Matching
item.description: arXiv:2610.12535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy-preserving order matching enables traders to discover and execute compatible orders while limiting disclosure of sensitive trading information. Existing systems span financial markets and blockchain-based asset exchanges and employ diverse market structures, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions, making their privacy guarantees difficult to compare. We present a systematization of privacy-preserving order matching covering 22 protocol families. We organize the order lifecycle into four phases: order representation and submission, order discovery and collection, order-matching, and settlement, and characterize each phase by protected and exposed information, access roles, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions. Our analysis shows that privacy is not a single protocol-level property: protecting selected order attributes or individual phases does not necessarily prevent leakage elsewhere in the lifecycle. We identify recurring trade-offs among privacy, functionality, trust, and verifiability, highlighting the challenge of achieving end-to-end privacy across the complete order lifecycle.
item.dc:creator: Prerna Arote, Adrian Saiz, Lucianna Kiffer

item.title: Organizational Context for the Enterprise Security Brain
item.description: arXiv:2610.12540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents that investigate and decide on enterprise security reason over a machine-readable view of the environment: its assets, identities, configurations, relations, and findings. The correct judgment about an asset also depends on what the organization knows about it: who owns it, what business function it serves, which policy governs it, and which risks were accepted. Part of this knowledge can be inferred from machine state, such as an ownership tag; most of it is recorded by people in policies, audit reports, architecture diagrams, tickets, and conversations, outside machine state. We call this distance the organizational context gap. Closing it poses four challenges: extracting the right claims from heterogeneous organizational data and, at inference time, detecting claims made stale by live state, checking live state against the governing policy, and binding architecture diagrams, which carry the business logic, to live resources. We introduce organizational context as a layer of the enterprise security brain and define it with a taxonomy and six properties its representation must preserve. We then define a context model in which a claim carries one meaning, an attestation records each source that asserts it, strength is derived from live evidence at read time, and claims resolve onto the entities of the asset graph. On a production environment spanning AWS, Okta, Google Workspace, and GitHub, extraction recovers 0.80 of a pooled 1,355-claim ground truth at 0.87 precision, with 0.5% of extracted claims unsupported by their source. An agent reasoning over live state and resolved context raises the conflict in 0.97 of stale-finding tasks, and reaches answer correctness of 0.83 on policy-alignment tasks and 0.86 on architecture tasks.
item.dc:creator: Eden Yavin, Ariel Zadok, Gal Engelberg, Elad Elouz, Leon Goldberg

item.title: HOMARD: Hammering Off-chip Memory via Aggregate power Rail Disclosure
item.description: arXiv:2610.12621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software-based microarchitectural attacks have mainly exploited timing differences to infer information from DRAM. However, defenses and optimizations can prevent timing-based approaches from resolving precise microarchitectural behaviors. We show that unprivileged millisecond- and milliampere-resolution power sensors on modern Arm SoCs can recover DRAM mapping functions and reveal the data dependence of memory accesses without timers. We present HOMARD, a methodology that reads DRAM activity from this telemetry, and two attack primitives. HOMARD-RE is a hierarchy-aware linear-algebraic method that reverse-engineers DRAM addressing functions from power alone. HOMARD-DATA recovers the Hamming weight of a fetched cache line through joint-power rail templating and secret byte values through correlation power analysis on the same rails. Across an AMD ZCU102, a Raspberry Pi 5, and a multi-chip-based LPDDR4 NVIDIA Jetson TX2, HOMARD-RE succeeds where row-buffer timing methods fail. On the Pi 5, HOMARD-DATA classifies 9 Hamming-weight levels at 81.5% accuracy and recovers secret bytes in minutes by correlating rail current with data-dependent bit toggling between neighbors in a row. Both primitives work with an architectural load or a mispredicted Spectre-RSB path on which no value is architecturally read. These results establish unprivileged power telemetry as an independent side channel for profiled microarchitectural attacks, particularly when timing falls silent.
item.dc:creator: Eliott Qu\'er\'e, Li-Chung Chiang, Carina Fiedler, Thomas Rokicki, Maria M\'endez Real, Alessandro Palumbo, Lilian Bossuet, Rub\'en Salvador, Daniel Gruss

item.title: Cancerous Backdoor Attack: Gradual Activation via Invisible Tokens and A Stage Controller
item.description: arXiv:2610.12644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Backdoor Attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) typically follow a trigger-response pattern, where satisfying a trigger condition activates a single terminal behavior. However, this single-point backdoor activation does not explore attacks in which malicious behavior develops gradually through multiple intermediate stages before reaching the terminal activation stage. We present Cancerous Backdoor Attack, that gradually corrupts an LLM's reasoning over a sequence of interactions by leveraging invisible tokens and a stage controller. Specifically, invisible tokens provide hidden stages to the model without appearing in the user's visible request and the stage controller tracks the attack's progression during inference to realize gradual activation. We evaluate Cancerous Backdoor Attack across several reasoning datasets. The attack consistently produces gradual reasoning corruption across models and tasks. We compare Cancerous Backdoor Attack with prior backdoor attack baselines to demonstrate our proposed attack outperforms the baselines. Our results indicate that reasoning corruption can develop gradually before it becomes visible, making answer accuracy alone insufficient for detecting backdoor attacks.
item.dc:creator: Tahmid Imtiaz Imu, Emama Nahid, Prodipta Sen Amartya, Ahsanul Jobayer, Yutong Song, Jiang Wu, Pengfei Zhang, Honghui Xu

item.title: Enabling Extended SGX Enclaves inside Confidential Virtual Machines
item.description: arXiv:2610.12695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs), such as AMD SEV-SNP, and process enclaves, such as Intel SGX, provide workload protection against cloud threats. However, they strongly differ in TCB, deployment cost and speed, peer workload protection, resource sharing, fine-grained isolation and attestation, and programming capabilities. Nesting process enclaves within CVMs offers an optimal solution and an opportunity to address long-standing SGX limitations: lack of intra-enclave protection, expensive transitions and exception paths, slow enclave cloning, and a restricted programming model that limits Library Operating Systems (LibOS). This paper introduces TEEVisor, a CVM-resident architecture consisting of a security monitor and a kernel driver that leverages AMD SEV-SNP Virtual Machine Privilege Levels (VMPLs) to build hardware-protected, process-level enclaves inside a guest CVM with two modes: (1) an SGX binary compatibility mode to run unmodified SGX applications; and (2) a novel extended SGX~(eSGX) mode optimizing slow execution paths and offering richer enclave programming capabilities. On commercial AMD EPYC hardware, against native CVM execution, TEEVisor incurs under 5% overhead on compute- and memory-bound workloads, around 12% on I/O-heavy applications, and accelerates enclave cloning to a rate of 93~$\mu$s/MB of enclave size, demonstrating that eSGX semantics inside a CVM are practical for production use.
item.dc:creator: Pamenas Kariuki, Dong Yiliang, Quoc Do Le, Christof Fetzer

item.title: PVBRF-ID: Private, Verifiable and Byzantine-Robust Federated Intrusion Detection for Oilfield Enterprise Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.12704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning allows dispersed oilfield sites to train a shared intrusion detector without pooling network traffic, yet its aggregation step forces a choice between privacy and robustness. Byzantine-robust rules must read each update in the clear, whereas secure aggregation hides updates from the checks that detect poisoning. We present PVBRF-ID, a two-server protocol in which sites secret-share their updates and the servers jointly test each update's norm and its cosine similarity to a reference computed on a small clean root set, revealing one accept bit per site. Commitments, Merkle roots and a homomorphic audit make the inclusion of accepted updates publicly verifiable. On a 15-class Edge-IIoTset task with ten sites holding differently distributed data and ten random seeds, PVBRF-ID matched FedAvg on clean data (macro-F1 0.708 vs. 0.706) and withstood sign-flip attacks (0.696 vs. 0.091). Against an adaptive attacker controlling 30% of sites, PVBRF-ID with secure clipping reached 0.641, whereas FedAvg fell to 0.046; plaintext multi-Krum remained higher by 0.052. An update-inference attacker recovered each site's class mix from plaintext updates (Spearman correlation 0.81) but not from one server's view. Backdoors passed the filter, and noise-based mitigation gave only heuristic protection. The implementation uses Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3, 30 rounds and 10 seeds.
item.dc:creator: Mustafa S. Aljumaily, Ali Ataeemh Allami, Mustafa N. Mnati, Nawar S. Alseelawi, Shahab Abdulla

item.title: Better Batches, Better Privacy: Random Allocation for DP-BandMF
item.description: arXiv:2610.12712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The current state of the art for batch selection and noise addition in differentially private training is a combination of DP-BandMF (informally, DP-SGD where the noise added in two different steps can be correlated if the steps are within $b$ of each other) and privacy amplification by sampling via Monte Carlo accounting. First, whereas prior batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF were inspired by Poisson sampling, random allocation is known to outperform Poisson sampling for DP-SGD. We therefore propose and analyze new batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF inspired by random allocation, improving RMSE by up to $1.85\times$ over previous work. Second, Monte Carlo accounting typically requires drawing $\Omega(1/\delta)$ samples from a privacy loss distribution, making accounting costly. We increase sampling and scoring throughput by two orders of magnitude through a carefully optimized GPU implementation. Finally, previous work chose the DP-BandMF strategy matrix and the batch selection strategy independently. We give a simple framework for choosing these parameters jointly, reducing RMSE by up to $13.4\%$ over fixed strategy matrices.
item.dc:creator: Ryan McKenna, Arun Ganesh

item.title: Onions in the ATmosphere: Decentralizing Trust in Identity
item.description: arXiv:2610.12764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiple approaches have been implemented for identities that associate meaningful identifiers, such as domain names, with self-authenticating identifiers, such as onion addresses. While these approaches offer various advantages both from identifier meaningfulness and from identifier self-authentication, identifier association itself is subject to blocking, hijack, fingerprinting, and other forms of surveillance and manipulation. So too are the resources associated with an identity comprising a meaningful identifier and a self-authenticating identifier. This paper describes ongoing work on two such approaches to self-authenticating meaningful identity (SAMI): associating a registered domain name with an onion address (onion association) and associating an atproto handle with a decentralized identifier (DID association). We present both the application of already implemented and published means of secure onion association to DID association and the combination of both in a single identity. Finally, we describe grounding identity association and integrity in contextual trust, wherein trusting attestations of identity relies on contextual relevance of an attestor to the identity rather than relying only on structural authority, for example as embodied in the traditional centralized infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Paul Syverson, Nick Gerakines

item.title: Power, Performance, and Area of HPC-Based Malware Detectors: An FPGA and Open-PDK ASIC Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.12795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware malware detectors (HMDs) classify programs as benign or malicious based on hardware performance counter (HPC) data. Previous studies have shown that ensemble classifiers outperform other classifiers on detection metrics. However, the area, power, and timing costs of HMDs remain open questions. We address these questions across a comprehensive design space comprising multiple classifier families, variable HPC sets, and ensemble learning methods. We designed a pipeline to reconstruct selected trained models, generate synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) implementations, validate each design against a bit-accurate golden model, and evaluate the implementations. The results show that tree- and rule-based detectors achieve the highest detection performance with nearly an order of magnitude less area and several times lower energy than function-based classifiers. Reducing the number of HPC inputs to fit a processor's concurrent-counter limit preserves detection performance while substantially reducing area, power, and delay.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Abolhasani Zeraatkar, Parnian Shabani Kamran, Parsa Mirfasihi, Saleh Khalaj Monfared, Hussain Al-Asaad

item.title: Vulnerable Models in the AI Supply Chain: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Propagation, and Usage Patterns
item.description: arXiv:2610.12893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has established a complex supply chain, but many of these shared artifacts harbor severe vulnerabilities such as insecure serialization and architectural backdoors. While prior efforts have extensively scanned model registries to flag malicious artifacts, a critical gap remains in understanding how developers actually adopt and integrate these unsafe models into downstream software systems. We bridge this gap by conducting a large-scale empirical study on the usage and propagation of 16,977 known vulnerable models on HuggingFace flagged by InsightDB. We track their prevalence across GitHub repositories, software packages, fine-tuning chains, and deployed applications. Our analysis reveals that, despite being publicly flagged, these vulnerable models appear in over 21,000 code locations across more than 5,000 open-source repositories, with 3,757 distinct flagged models (22.1\%) actively referenced in at least one project. To understand how these models are integrated in code and identify recurring usage patterns, we categorize and analyze the recurring patterns surrounding them via a customized pipeline that combines Code Property Graphs extraction with a tailored Frequent Subgraph Mining approach. Across all patterns, we find no evidence of provenance verification or model sanitization logic, with developers frequently bypassing security parameters or delegating trust to permissive framework defaults. These findings underscore that scanning model files alone is insufficient, highlighting the urgent need for context-aware security analysis and stricter integration guardrails at the application layer of the AI supply chain.
item.dc:creator: The Anh Nguyen, Triet Huynh Minh Le, M. Ali Babar

item.title: Sample-Preserving Search-to-Decision Reduction for Noisy Linear Equations over Large Moduli
item.description: arXiv:2610.12913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Noisy Linear Equations problem involves finding the solution to a random linear system over a finite field given noisy evaluations. This is a generalisation of various learning problems widely used in cryptography, including Learning with Errors (LWE), Learning with Rounding (LWR), and Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). We present a new sample-preserving search-to-decision reduction for Noisy Linear Equations that has complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log q, q/\sigma)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the secret, $m$ is the number of samples, $q$ is the modulus, and $\sigma$ is the magnitude of the noise (defined suitably for the kind of noise involved). In particular, this implies search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR that run in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ even if the modulus $q$ is exponentially large, as long as the noise-to-modulus ratio $\sigma/q$ is non-negligible. Our reduction works for prime moduli $q$. If $q$ is composite, it instead produces a list that contains a small multiple of the solution. Prior to this work, known search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR either did not preserve the parameters of the problem (i.e., $m$, $n$, $\sigma$, and $q$), or had complexity that scaled polynomially with either $\sigma$ or the largest prime factor of $q$.
item.dc:creator: Andrej Bogdanov, Kel Zin Tan, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan

item.title: AgentValve: Sybil-Resilient Payment Authorization for Permissionless AI Markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.12948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents increasingly select and pay service providers without human review. In emerging permissionless markets, however, adversaries can create inexpensive identities and fabricate feedback to inflate provider reputation, making reputation-based payment authorization vulnerable to Sybil attacks and exposing clients to unbounded financial loss. This paper presents AgentValve, a protocol for Sybil-resilient payment authorization in permissionless AI markets. AgentValve builds on a trust network that represents reputation as finite capacity in a directed graph and authorizes payments through trust paths with sufficient available capacity. A smart contract atomically reserves the capacity supporting each admitted payment, bounding honest agents' payment exposure by the capacity they extend into the adversarial region, and thus creating identities or interactions entirely within that region cannot increase this bound. To limit capacity depletion by malicious senders, AgentValve combines payment-backed capacity creation with bounded route length, preventing attackers from depleting honest capacity without incurring corresponding payment costs. AgentValve further decouples off-chain route discovery from on-chain verification and introduces a witness-commit mechanism that reduces route verification to linear work while requiring only constant persistent state per admitted payment. We implement a AgentValve prototype and evaluate it using six months of Ethereum data and synthetic workloads. Experimental results show that under attacks with up to 10,000 synthetic Sybil identities and with chosen attackers, the payment exposure and capacity depletion remain bounded. Regarding practicality, the witness-commit mechanism lowers admission cost by up to 40.8% compared with baselines, and admitting common payments costs approximately \$0.04-\$0.21.
item.dc:creator: Jianting Zhang, Zhongtang Luo, Aniket Kate

item.title: WaveMark: Robust Wavelet-Domain Image Watermarking for Diffusion Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.12952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Image watermarking enables provenance tracing for photorealistic images generated by diffusion models. However, state-of-the-art (SOTA) removal attacks can suppress embedded signals with little perceptual degradation. This vulnerability limits the effectiveness of watermarks for intellectual property protection and misuse attribution. We propose WaveMark, a novel wavelet-domain watermarking method that embeds messages in a diffusion model's initial noise. To support robust recovery from perturbed carriers, WaveMark distributes keyed replicas of message bits across spatial positions, wavelet orientations, and scales. Each carrier groups coefficients from four latent channels and encodes a randomized bit through magnitude projection, providing an explicit decoding margin. We evaluate WaveMark with SD2.1 on SDP and MS-COCO Captions under 14 attacks. WaveMark achieves 100.0% bit accuracy (BA) without attacks, while maintaining image quality comparable to the evaluated baselines. Under SOTA MarkNull and MarkNull-A, it retains over 88% BA, outperforming all baselines.
item.dc:creator: Jie Cao, Qi Li, Chaklam Cheong, Yutong Jin, Enze Yu, Zelin Zhang, Jianbing Ni

item.title: Post-Quantum Session Establishment for Matter over Thread: Message Size, Transport, and Protocol Options
item.description: arXiv:2610.13026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matter's first post-quantum change protects device attestation with ML-DSA, but its operational handshake, CASE, still derives session keys from P-256 ECDH, so recorded traffic can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. We quantify the cost of moving CASE to ML-KEM and post-quantum signatures over Thread, where frames carry at most 127 bytes and a Matter message at most 1178 bytes. A byte-exact model of the CASE messages shows that a drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB and that no fully post-quantum configuration built from FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms fits the message limit. A Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter source constants, shows that sending these messages as fragmented IPv6 datagrams causes spurious retransmissions whenever a message and its reply outlast Matter's retransmission timer. At three to four hops the drop-in handshake then takes 1.8 to 2.6 times longer than with a selective-repeat block transfer, with or without interference, and up to 33% of handshakes with sleepy devices fail; raising the timers does not remove the effect. Caching certificate chains and authenticating the device with a pre-distributed ML-KEM key reduce the handshake to 6.1 kB and 44 ms of device computation. As a first step, hybrid P-256+ML-KEM-512 key exchange with a cached device chain protects session keys against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks while every message still fits the current limit.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Commey

item.title: Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
item.description: arXiv:2610.13043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, for any fixed $\kappa>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, the same time bound holds with errors bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ and only $O(n/\ln\ln q)$ samples. Earlier, it was known that Kirchner and Fouque's algorithm could solve LWE with these parameters in subexponential time with a much larger number of samples $m = \Omega(n\log{n})$ [HKM18]. Ducas et al. [DEL25] showed that an adaptation of this algorithm could solve the corresponding dual, the $\mathrm{SIS}^{\infty}$ problem, with a suitable norm bound $q/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ and $m=n+\omega(n/\ln\ln n)$ variables in subexponential time. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.
item.dc:creator: Haoxing Lin, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan

item.title: Space Over Statistic, Retraining Over Ranking: Auditing Training Labels Under Label-Only Backdoors
item.description: arXiv:2610.13051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Some backdoor attacks never touch an image. FLIP only changes labels: on CIFAR-10, flipping 3% of them makes a ResNet-32 send 99.7% of triggered source-class images to the attacker's class. The usual defenses look for the poison inside a model trained on those same labels. So when they struggle, is the problem the test they run, or the space they run it in? We answer with a controlled swap: we keep the test, the labels and the metric fixed, change only the feature space, and judge each defense by retraining the victim on what it keeps. The space decides. On dog$\to$cat the same nearest-neighbor check scores AUROC 0.546 on the poisoned model's features, 0.967 on frozen DINOv2 features that never saw a label, and 0.995 on the same network trained on clean labels, an oracle control rather than a defense. We reproduce SPECTRE, the defense FLIP's authors recommend, to 90.94 / 0.97 against its published 91.47 / 1.7, then price it: on truck$\to$deer it deletes 20% of every class, while a prototype audit on the frozen features deletes 6% for higher clean accuracy and lower attack success. On three harder pairs that audit leaves about a quarter of the attack standing. A count read off encoder geometry and clean labels, before any attack is run, separates the pair where the audit removes the attack from those where it only partly does, though on a single zero-count pair. Three results warn against the easy story. A better detection score does not mean a safer model: on two of four pairs Confident Learning scores the higher AUROC, and on dog$\to$cat leaves 2.6 times the attack success. The prototype family, our best static performer, is the first an adaptive attacker slips past. And past a point, catching more poisons stops reducing attack success. Check labels in a space that never learned them, and judge a defense by the retrained model, not by its detection score.
item.dc:creator: Arnab Dey, Mohammad Mahfuzul Islam

item.title: CAPE - Context-Aware Prioritization Engine for Vulnerability Scoring and Management
item.description: arXiv:2610.13071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability patching is critical for safeguarding an enterprise's software ecosystem from cyber attacks. However, patching requires adequate preparation for potential system downtime and for unforeseen effects of the patched software on a live system. Thus, effective risk mitigation requires prioritization strategies that explicitly account for the operational context of the affected software. While vulnerability prioritization based on Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, can help, their differing goals and methodologies often lead to inconsistent, context-unaware decisions resulting in mis-allocated remediation efforts. In this work, we present the Context-Aware Prioritization Engine (CAPE), a vulnerability analysis framework that enriches each vulnerability scanner report of vulnerabilities (CVEs) with deployment-specific evidence. This evidence is used to perform vulnerability reachability, centrality, and exploitability analysis, producing a ranked priority score for the effective distribution of remediation effort. We evaluate CAPE on 30 open-source agentic applications comprising 6,138 scanner-reported CVEs. Our evaluation shows that a significant majority of CVEs are not reachable and exploitable which results in significant disparities between CAPE and context-free baselines - the CVSS, EPSS, and KEV. It also shows that CAPE consistently surfaces confirmed-exploitable CVEs at higher priority than all baselines, demonstrating that context-aware analysis provides substantially more accurate remediation guidance than context-free severity scoring alone.
item.dc:creator: Rakesh Podder, Viktoria Koscinski, Indrajit Ray

item.title: The Limits of Query Monitoring against Distributed Model Extraction
item.description: arXiv:2610.13083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model providers now face distillation campaigns run through thousands of accounts, each of which looks like an ordinary user. When network and payment metadata cannot link those accounts, the only evidence left is what they ask. We study what a provider can and cannot learn from those queries alone, using one million real chat turns for development and 17 later weeks that no design choice touched for a single frozen evaluation. The answer is set less by anything specific to extraction than by benign coordination: a campaign is visible only if it is more distinctive than the most distinctive group of ordinary users in the same week. We make this precise, show that a small but positive difference between campaign and users buys a detection time rather than detectability, and identify the campaign that is hardest to detect. Empirically, a calibrated monitor catches naive distributed extraction that per-account monitors miss (0.86-1.00 of weeks), and one variant - selecting accounts that move together after discounting how topical each one is - still catches campaigns padded with natural text (0.50-0.96 of weeks) where the other two spectral detectors catch none. Distilling each campaign into a small student shows that, in our testbed, campaigns that evaded every detector kept at most 42% of the capability of a detectable one. The limits are equally concrete: a campaign that ramps up slowly poisons every detector's calibration, benign evaluation pipelines look exactly like distillation, we found no deployable detector at colluder shares of 2.5% or below, and campaigns that relay real users' requests may be invisible to any query-only monitor.
item.dc:creator: Snigdha Chandan Khilar

item.title: Safety Graph: When Safety Responses Become Attack Surfaces in Cyber-Physical Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.13086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern industrial control systems (ICS) are susceptible to cyber attacks triggering safety failures in the operational technology (OT) layer. The traditional way to mitigate any failure in OT is to implement safety responses. However, we show in this work that these responses can open up new attack surfaces, thereby vastly expanding the scope of lateral movement. Existing frameworks model cyber-to-physical escalation but provide no mechanism to reason about how these safety responses to OT-failures can trigger new cascading cyber attacks in the Information Technology (IT) layer. To enable such reasoning, we introduce Safety Graph (SG), a formal framework unifying three paradigms - Attack Graphs (AG), Fault Trees (FT), and Event Trees (ET) - over a shared propositional state space, capturing the full bidirectional IT-OT cascade. We provide a sound and complete compilation of SG to a classical AI planning problem, performing plan search using A* to find cross-layer cascade paths. Through a Web3D modeling and simulation of the Tennessee Eastman chemical process plant, which is a widely used chemical engineering benchmark serving as a standard for testing control, monitoring and fault propagation, we demonstrate that the planning compilation of SG automatically discovers safety-response-induced lateral movements, and identifies the responsible barriers that are unidentifiable under existing models. A complexity and scalability analysis characterizes how the planning compilation of SG scales with model size and cascade depth. To the best of our knowledge, SG is the first framework to formally model IT-OT attacks and enable operators to explore the problem of cyber attacks triggering cascading failures in ICS.
item.dc:creator: Rakesh Podder, Philip D. Hopkins, Sarath Sreedharan, Indrakshi Ray, Indrajit Ray

item.title: Understanding Verification Vulnerabilities in Cross-chain Bridges: An Empirical Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.13170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid development of blockchain technology, numerous heterogeneous blockchains have emerged, each featuring distinct architectures, consensus mechanisms, and application ecosystems. Cross-chain bridges have consequently become a critical infrastructure component, typically relying on smart contracts to facilitate message passing and asset transfers across heterogeneous blockchains. Unlike single-chain contracts, bridge contracts introduce additional verification logic to validate external-chain data, such as state proofs, message sender identities, and signatures. However, correctly implementing such logic is challenging. We refer to vulnerabilities that violate the security guarantees of cross-chain verification as Cross-chain Verification Vulnerabilities (CVVs). To characterize CVVs, we conduct the first systematic empirical study of this vulnerability class. By analyzing 588 security audit reports from 36 real-world cross-chain bridge projects, we derive 11 CVV patterns and organize them into 5 high-level categories according to the affected verification properties. Following this taxonomy, we construct a CVV dataset containing 830 vulnerability instances across 786 contract files. The dataset establishes mappings among audit reports, audited source-code versions, affected source files, and CVV-pattern labels. We then assess existing detection approaches. Current tools provide limited documented coverage of CVV patterns, while only two of four evaluated LLMs outperform an all-pattern constant baseline of 29.3% Macro-F1; the best reaches 51.2%. Together, the limited tool coverage and inconsistent LLM gains motivate detection methods tailored to cross-chain verification semantics.
item.dc:creator: Yuying Wang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China), Yi Guo (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China), Jiachi Chen (The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain,Data Security, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou High-Tech Zone), Hanwen Zhang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China), Yi Sun (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China)

item.title: Understanding and Mitigating Cross-Session Attacks via Persistent Artifacts in Agent Skill Composition
item.description: arXiv:2610.13227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills extend the capabilities of AI agents by bundling instructions, code, and resources into reusable packages. During skill execution, agents may produce or modify artifacts, such as files, configurations, and cached data, that are reused by other skills in later sessions. Since these artifacts can persist across sessions and later be accessed by other skills, they introduce a new attack surface that can be exploited to influence subsequent executions. However, the security risks arising from such cross-session skill interactions remain largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate cross-session composition attacks in skill-based AI agents and develop a runtime defense against them. Specifically, we characterize three attack mechanisms, namely Instruction Propagation (IP), Data Boundary Violation (DBV), and Evidence Poisoning (EP), through which malicious effects propagate across skill executions via persistent artifacts. To evaluate whether existing agents can resist these attacks while completing legitimate tasks, we construct SkillRelayBench, a benchmark of 270 adversarial cases drawn from 30 cross-session skill-composition scenarios across ten domains. Our evaluation of seven models across Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code reveals attack success rates (ASR) ranging from 46.7% to 77.4% and attack chain success rates (ACSR) ranging from 35.6% to 61.1%. Successful attack chains cover all five target security consequence categories, highlighting the broad impact of these attacks. To mitigate these risks, we propose SkillRelayGuard, which restores artifact provenance context and provides pre-execution advisory review while leaving the final execution decision to the agent. Evaluation across three agent settings shows that SkillRelayGuard reduces overall ASR from 69.5% to 10.9% and ACSR from 54.8% to 10.0%, while increasing legitimate task completion from 79.6% to 87.5%.
item.dc:creator: Dianshu Liao, Shidong Pan, Guangdong Bai, Zhenchang Xing, Xiaoyu Sun

item.title: Quantization-Tolerant Gradient Auditing for Active Inference-Attack Detection in Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.13311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inside a federated learning system a participant can quietly study the shared model and learn about others' private data. The usual defense, differential privacy, often adds so much noise that the model is no longer worth training. In cross-silo FL, where participants are a few accountable organizations and the server is trusted, we ask whether the server can instead interrogate clients. Each round it sends a secret challenge batch and asks every client to return a checksum of the gradient that batch induces, together with a timing. A client that mutated the model state, as an active generative-adversarial-network discriminator attacker does, returns a wrong checksum. We make this checksum robust to benign cross-platform floating-point non-determinism with a quantized fingerprint compared under a small tolerance. It flags two distinct active attacks at a true-positive rate of $1.0$ with no false positives on the checksum axis, stable across the fingerprint's parameters and up to $50$ clients at malicious ratios to $40\%$, for $32\,\mathrm{ms}$ of server work and $4.35\,\mathrm{kB}$ per response. Against a purely passive attacker the only signal is timing, and it is not robust: a cohort-relative test detects only in low-jitter conditions while a false-positive-free per-client baseline is blind, so no configuration delivers both. An attacker that answers the challenge on an untouched copy of the model while tampering with a replica evades the audit entirely. Therefore the checksum is a reliable in-band signal against attackers that do not decouple the audited computation from the attacked one, and it composes with differential privacy, whose accuracy cost we quantify on Texas100, rather than replacing it.
item.dc:creator: Michael Kuehne-Schlinkert

item.title: Secrets in Preamble: Practical and Robust PHY Information Hiding for Wi-Fi
item.description: arXiv:2610.13367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical layer (PHY) information hiding refers to the concealment of secrets within PHY waveforms without compromising the integrity of the primary communication link, thereby enabling critical applications such as covert communication, PHY steganography, and watermarking. The widespread deployment of Wi-Fi has motivated substantial research interest in hiding secrets within Wi-Fi waveforms. However, existing Wi-Fi information hiding approaches suffer from two limitations: restricted steganographic capacity and insufficient robustness against environmental variations, both of which severely constrain practical deployment. This work proposes to embed secrets within the Wi-Fi legacy short training field (L-STF). The designed method preserves the autocorrelation properties of Wi-Fi L-STF, ensuring that packet detection and coarse frequency offset compensation functionalities remain uncompromised. The secret embedding and extraction processes employ a pair of neural networks designed to learn optimal embedding rules and maximize steganographic capacity. We developed a prototype system and conducted comprehensive experiments across both indoor and outdoor environments. Experimental results show that our method can reliably embed 46 secret bits within Wi-Fi packets across diverse channel conditions, achieving significantly enhanced steganographic capacity and environmental robustness. The hardware prototype study validates the feasibility of the proposed Wi-Fi information hiding scheme.
item.dc:creator: Rui Pan, Guanxiong Shen, Linning Peng, Xinyu Qi, Junqing Zhang

item.title: Towards Safe World Models: Risks, Defenses, and Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2610.13372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models support planning, control, learning from imagined experience, and model-mediated evaluation by predicting action-conditioned consequences. Their safety cannot be inferred from predictive accuracy alone: errors in observations, state and memory, dynamics, evaluation, execution, or feedback can propagate into unsafe decisions and persist through updates. This work organizes the literature on world-model safety around a six-stage lifecycle covering data and observations, state and memory, dynamics and imagination, evaluation and planning, action and control, and feedback and update. We synthesize non-adversarial failures, attacks, defenses, evaluation protocols, benchmarks, and deployment conditions, and distinguish evidence directness from outcome level. The current evidence corpus contains 163 cited works. We use the framework to identify where claims are supported, where attribution remains unresolved, and which measurements are needed to connect model-level behavior to closed-loop and operational safety.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoma Wang, Litian Zhang, Xinze Shi, Zhengxuan Hu, Zihan Yang, Mingqi Ren, You Wu, Bingyu Yan, Zelong Yu, Zhenjie Su, Yuming Shang, Xi Zhang, Chaozhuo Li, Philip S. Yu

item.title: EviRepair: Evidence-Driven Agents for Reliable Vulnerability Repair
item.description: arXiv:2610.13491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agent-based approaches for repository-level automated vulnerability repair (AVR), showing promising repair capabilities. However, an important issue has received limited attention: how can we ensure that the evidence generated during the repair process is reliable enough to support accurate vulnerability understanding and patch generation? In this paper, we propose EviRepair, an evidence-driven multi-agent framework for repository-level AVR. EviRepair introduces evidence review into the repair process by enabling agents to collaboratively collect vulnerability evidence, verify evidence consistency, and construct a reviewed vulnerability model for patch synthesis and validation. Extensive experiments on PatchEval and SecBench benchmarks with multiple agent frameworks and LLMs demonstrate that EviRepair consistently outperforms existing agent-based baselines, achieving average improvements of 16.37% and 40.33% in resolved rates on PatchEval and SecBench, respectively. Codes are available at https://github.com/lly-s/EviRepair
item.dc:creator: Yilian Shi, Qingyu Liu, Tianyi Zhou, Wende Tan, Chenyang Si, Yueming Lyu, Xia Hu, Dongrui Liu

item.title: A Systematic Study of Security Enforcement at Android Inter-Component Boundaries
item.description: arXiv:2610.13597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Android's inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms (Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers, ContentProviders, and URI scheme handlers) form the primary interface between applications and between applications and the system. We present a systematic study of security enforcement comprising 120 evaluations (99 inter-component interface evaluations across five interface categories, 10 platform security-control evaluations, and 11 dedicated positive controls) in over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17 (API 37). Using an expected-versus-observed framework under a zero-permission attacker model, we evaluate whether each boundary's enforcement mechanism functions as designed. We find 97 enforcement gaps (80.8%) and 23 enforcement holds (19.2%). From these observations, we derive a 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy organized across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers. Within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories: evaluated Activities and BroadcastReceivers exhibit a 100% gap rate, while ContentProviders, which benefit from framework-provided defenses such as setStrict(), achieve a 27.6% holds rate. We find that all seven evaluated platform compatibility changes with security intent are either disabled or gated at a targetSdkVersion that none of the applications in our evaluated corpus targets. We document 18 custom URI scheme registrations handling sensitive data (authentication tokens, payment credentials, medical information) despite the known unverifiability of custom schemes (RFC 8252 Section 8.1). Our study includes 23 positive controls, calibration cases demonstrating that the evaluation procedure distinguishes functioning enforcement from observed enforcement failures.
item.dc:creator: Sandiyo Christan A

item.title: APEX-Harm: Evaluating Agent Safety in Shared Professional Workspaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.13623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Professional agents increasingly work through command-line interfaces and multiple tools over shared workspaces containing files, messages, and business applications. These environments create safety risks that are difficult to capture with attacks placed at a single, known read location. We introduce APEX-Harm, a benchmark for evaluating prompt and script injection against long-horizon agents performing finance, consulting, and legal tasks in large workspaces. Each task contains 115 to 328 files, together with email, calendar, chat, document, spreadsheet, PDF, and code-execution tools exposed through MCP servers. The benchmark includes six attack categories covering static and dynamic injections, task-specific script replacement, and attacker-provided generic scripts, and evaluates attack success, exposure, and task performance. We evaluate 12 frontier models on 180 task instances per model. Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 have the lowest overall attack success rates (8% and 20%), while task-specific script replacement and attacker-provided generic script attacks remain substantially more effective, averaging 81-84% and 73% attack success, respectively. Gemini 3.8 Flash achieves the highest mean task score (0.877) while still exhibiting a 33% attack success rate. These results show that completing the requested task is not sufficient evidence of safe behavior: an agent can produce a correct deliverable while also performing an unauthorized action in the workspace.
item.dc:creator: Ziyi Yang, Adel Bibi, Guohao Li, Bernard Ghanem, Carlos Hinojosa

item.title: ToFu: Exploiting and Fuzzing the LLM-Orchestrator-Tool Trust Boundary
item.description: arXiv:2610.13651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with external software through tools, with an orchestration layer translating model outputs into structured tool invocations. This architecture creates an LLM-orchestrator-tool trust boundary where tool semantics may go unenforced and LLM-generated arguments may be incorrectly treated as trusted. We present ToFu, a tool-aware framework that automatically derives semantic security checks for LLM tools from their existing metadata and a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus. ToFu specializes these checks to individual tools and automatically generates fuzzing harnesses and semantic oracles using runtime introspection and outcome sanitization. We evaluated ToFu across 273 MCP servers containing 3405 tools and identified verified bugs corresponding to CWE weakness classes in 343 tools across 118 of the servers. Our findings show that real-world tools frequently fail to enforce their documented input semantics, making it unsafe to treat LLM-generated arguments as trusted.
item.dc:creator: Md Nazmul Islam Ananto, Pierre Prevost-Avenel, Colin Smith, Kyungtae Kim, Taegyu Kim, Arslan Khan

item.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Cyber-Physical Risk-Aware Power Grid Operations
item.description: arXiv:2610.13853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power grid cyber-physical security requires intrusion detection methods that account for the operational consequences of detection errors. However, the existing intrusion detection approaches primarily focus on the predictive performance of learning algorithms, while downstream operational costs are often optimized independently, which can lead to inferior operational performance. To help alleviate this problem, we propose a novel optimization-learning cyber-physical-risk-informed framework that communicates iteratively to minimize power grid operational costs. This framework translates machine learning prediction errors into power grid operational cyber-physical-risk costs. Experimental results on two power grid operation datasets, Industrial Control System (ICS) Cyber Attack and Sherlock, show that the proposed approach improves power grid operation costs compared with the traditional approach.
item.dc:creator: Ayesha Siddiqua Dina, Ebisa D. Wollega, Afzal Hossain Sohag

item.title: Byzantine-Resilient Federated Large Language Model via Hypergraph Message Passing
item.description: arXiv:2610.12711v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated Large Language Models (FedLLMs) are promising to deliver privacy-preserving, collaborative intelligence. The decentralized training process is vulnerable to Byzantine attacks that corrupt semantic consistency and factual resilience through malicious model updates. This paper presents a new resilience strategy that prevents semantically corrupted knowledge from propagating during federated aggregation. A defense problem is formulated to jointly maximize global accuracy and suppress manipulated model updates, enabling trustworthy knowledge aggregation without accessing private local data. To strengthen the resilience of FedLLMs, we develop a novel Hypergraph Message Passing Graph Autoencoder (HMP-GAE) framework, where low-rank model updates are represented as nodes in a hypergraph and high-order semantic relationships among multiple agents are exploited through iterative message passing. By leveraging historical checkpoints and cross-agent relational reasoning, HMP-GAE identifies and suppresses semantically inconsistent updates while preserving knowledge alignment among agents throughout federated training. HMP-GAE is implemented using Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.2 as pretrained FedLLM backbones and evaluated on AG News and Yahoo! Answers datasets. Compared to existing defenses, HMP-GAE improves global accuracy by $1.21$\%, reduces final-model classification semantic entropy by $44.08$\%, and lowers perplexity by $13.34$\%. HMP-GAE outperforms the GAE-based defense by improving the accuracy $1.39$\%, reducing the semantic entropy by $54.5$\%, and lowering perplexity by $35.5$\%.
item.dc:creator: Kai Li, Hanlin Cai, Zihao Liu, Yichen Li, Jose Alcaraz Calero, Wei Ni, Falko Dressler, \"Ozg\"ur B. Akan

item.title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
item.description: arXiv:2610.12813v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over sensitive resources, such as private documents and mutable system states, which can create serious safety and security risks. Runtime guardrails should therefore make inspectable, reproducible, and deterministic allow or refuse decisions before potentially irreversible agent actions are executed. However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.
item.dc:creator: Duy Nguyen, Lesly Miculicich, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Shuo Li, Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham, Mohit Bansal, Tomas Pfister, Long T. Le

item.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.12822v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.
item.dc:creator: Yuepeng Hu, Pegah Ghahremani, Reza Aghajani, Mahesh Pasupuleti, Himaghna Bhattacharjee

item.title: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.12858v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: "Security by obscurity," or the idea that hiding how a system works helps protect it from adversaries, has long been poorly regarded in the security community. Yet its intuitive appeal persists, and it has resurfaced repeatedly in industry practices and public debates over the years. The logic, on the one hand, is that open scrutiny of systems is the best way to find and respond to problems; and on the other hand, that too much openness can increase risk by giving adversaries a roadmap for attack. This isn't purely a technical question, but a human one: it's about how attackers and good-faith security researchers respond to openness in the real world. As such, security experts base their stance on decades of community experience; however, the field lacks empirical or theoretical foundations to back up these long-standing beliefs. We provide the first rigorous modeling of "security by obscurity," aiming to capture how rational actors will respond to openness or obscurity in fallible systems. We prove that in equilibrium under realistic model conditions, "obscured" systems are more likely to suffer successful attacks than "open" systems --- establishing theoretical support for the longstanding received wisdom.
item.dc:creator: In-Uck Park, Sunoo Park

item.title: LETHE: Defending against Unauthorized Image-to-Video Generation via Value Diversity Collapse
item.description: arXiv:2610.13333v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models can animate a single reference image into high-quality, subject-consistent videos, posing threats of misuse as anyone can turn personal photos into fabricated videos without consent. A promising solution is to proactively add an adversarial perturbation to the image before release, such that videos generated from it would be unfaithful or visually corrupted. However, due to an insufficient understanding of what governs how subsequent frames read the reference image in modern I2V models, existing protections struggle to offer strong protection under common perturbation budgets. In this paper, we approach the problem by exploring this underlying reading mechanism. Through a convex geometric analysis, we theoretically identify the spread of the reference value vectors as a key factor governing this reading process, and empirically find that even a mild contraction of this spread can severely degrade the generated video, making it an efficient lever for protection. Guided by this insight, we propose LETHE, a novel protection method that directly disrupts this reading process. LETHE pairs two complementary objectives, where a value collapse objective drives the reference value vectors toward uniformity, while an attention attraction objective draws subsequent frames toward these collapsed tokens to amplify corruption. We further construct two human-centric I2V protection benchmarks and conduct extensive experiments with multiple modern I2V models, which demonstrate the state-of-the-art protection performance and versatility of LETHE.
item.dc:creator: Boheng Li, Yueming Xing, Yiming Li, Jie Zhang, Tianwei Zhang

item.title: ECGWmark: Deep Watermarking for Electrocardiogram Signals
item.description: arXiv:2610.13357v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Secure transmission of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals remains a major challenge in telecardiology. While traditional mathematical watermarking can embed patient metadata directly into ECG signals, it is highly fragile against temporal desynchronization such as circular phase shifts. In contrast, existing deep watermarking approaches for temporal signals, such as audio, typically rely on lossy quantization, which compromises the high-frequency micro-morphological details critical for clinical diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we propose ECGWmark, a fully convolutional and quantization-free deep watermarking framework for medical time-series. ECGWmark operates in a continuous, full-resolution latent space and utilizes a localized frame-level mechanism to improve the robustness to severe desynchronization. Crucially, we introduce a differentiable Physiological Loss guided by a clinical classifier to preserve diagnostic semantics. Experiments on the benchmark MIT-BIH database show that ECGWmark maintains channel-bit extraction accuracy above 90% under the evaluated circular temporal shifts. Furthermore, under a rigorous inter-patient diagnostic evaluation, Class-V sensitivity changes from 71.97% to 76.50%, whereas Macro-F1 changes from 35.25% to 34.71% and Class-S sensitivity from 8.89% to 1.39%; these results indicate mixed class-level effects.
item.dc:creator: Kuan-Yu Chen, Kuan-Chen Wang, Yu Tsao, Jian-Jiun Ding

item.title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
item.description: arXiv:2610.13928v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task - a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.
item.dc:creator: Andis Draguns, Sumeet Ramesh Motwani, Raymond Douglas, Christian Schroeder de Witt

item.title: Auditing Prompt Injection Defenses Before They Reach Users: What Strong Adversaries Reveal
item.description: arXiv:2505.15738v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in user-facing products that handle sensitive personal data while interacting with untrusted external content. This makes them a prime target for prompt injection attacks, in which an adversary injects malicious instructions in that content to hijack the model. Fine-tuning-based defenses have been proposed to mitigate these attacks by training models to follow benign user instructions and ignore injected ones. Lacking formal guarantees, these defenses are evaluated empirically against the most effective realistic attacks available at the time, often reporting near-zero attack success rates -- giving developers, and the users who depend on them, a false sense of security and leaving open the possibility that future, more capable attacks could circumvent them and cause severe consequences in widely deployed systems. In this paper, we argue that developers should stress-test their defenses before release, and we introduce an auditing framework that does so without requiring defenders to invent the next state-of-the-art attack. Our key insight is that the fine-tuning process itself yields useful artifacts: intermediate checkpoints that serve as stepping stones for optimization-based attacks. Although these artifacts are unavailable to real attackers, we show that the vulnerabilities they expose are genuine and can be exploited by realistic adversaries. Instantiating our framework with optimization-based attacks such as GCG and BEAST, we raise attack success rates against state-of-the-art defenses from near zero to as high as 96\%, revealing weaknesses missed by prior evaluations. Our results show that current evaluation practices can substantially overestimate robustness, and that auditing defenses under strong adversaries before deployment shortens the feedback loop and helps prevent attacks from causing real-world harm to users.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoxue Yang, Bozhidar Stevanoski, Matthieu Meeus, Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye

item.title: LLMail-Inject: A Dataset from a Realistic Adaptive Prompt Injection Challenge
item.description: arXiv:2506.09956v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Indirect prompt injection attacks exploit a fundamental weakness of LLMs: executing unauthorized tasks from untrusted sources. Despite the practical significance of this attack vector, existing benchmarks rely on small sets of template-based attacks (100-1,000 examples) that fail to capture the diversity and adaptiveness of real-world adversaries. Consequently, benchmarks are saturated and overfit to static attacks. We introduce LLMail-Inject, a large-scale benchmark of 208,095 distinct human-written attack prompts collected through a public red-teaming challenge with 839 participants. LLMail-Inject evaluates the attack's complete chain of execution: prompts must be retrieved from an email database, evade production-level defenses, and trigger unauthorized tool calls with correct arguments. Evaluation reveals that models that achieve 5% attack success rate (ASR) on existing benchmarks fail more on LLMail-Inject: Meta SecAlign--specifically trained against prompt injection--still yields 32% ASR, GPT-4o exhibits 58% ASR, and GPT-5 mini 47% ASR. We further demonstrate that attacks transfer across domains, achieving 37% ASR on proof-of-concept coding tasks and 28-45% ASR on file management tasks. We release our challenge platform and curated evaluation subsets at multiple difficulty tiers and the full dataset with rich annotations.
item.dc:creator: Sahar Abdelnabi, Aideen Fay, Ahmed Salem, Egor Zverev, Kai-Chieh Liao, Chi-Huang Liu, Chun-Chih Kuo, Jannis Weigend, Danyael Manlangit, Alex Apostolov, Haris Umair, Jo\~ao Donato, Masayuki Kawakita, Athar Mahboob, Tran Huu Bach, Tsun-Han Chiang, Myeongjin Cho, Hajin Choi, Byeonghyeon Kim, Hyeonjin Lee, Benjamin Pannell, Conor McCauley, Mark Russinovich, Andrew Paverd, Giovanni Cherubin

item.title: The Express Lane to Spam and Centralization: An Empirical Analysis of Arbitrum's Timeboost
item.description: arXiv:2509.22143v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: DeFi applications are vulnerable to MEV, where specialized actors profit by reordering or inserting transactions. To mitigate latency races and internalize MEV revenue, Arbitrum introduced Timeboost, an auction-based transaction sequencing mechanism that grants short-term priority access to an express lane. In this paper, we present the first large-scale empirical study of Timeboost, analyzing over 48.5 million express lane transactions and 494 thousand auctions between January 2025 and April 2026. Our results reveal five main findings. First, express lane control is highly centralized, with three entities winning 99.74% of auctions. Second, while express lane access provides earlier inclusion, it is currently mainly used for CEX-DEX arbitrage, limiting the value of priority access for other types of MEV extraction. Third, approximately 30% of timeboosted transactions revert, indicating that Timeboost does not effectively mitigate MEV inefficiencies such as spam. Fourth, secondary markets for reselling express lane rights struggle to sustain themselves due to poor execution reliability and unsustainable economics. Finally, auction competition declined as secondary markets introduced dedicated CEX-DEX execution lanes, enabling pay-per-transaction instead of pay-per-round billing and leading to steadily reduced revenue for the Arbitrum DAO. Taken together, these findings show that Timeboost fails to deliver on its stated goals of fairness, decentralization, and internalizing long term revenue for the DAO. Instead, it currently allows for collusion and narrows adoption, highlighting the limitations of auction-based ordering as a mechanism for fair transaction sequencing in rollups.
item.dc:creator: Johnnatan Messias, Christof Ferreira Torres

item.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Website Fingerprinting Attacks and Defenses in Tor: Advances and Open Challenges
item.description: arXiv:2510.11804v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Tor network provides users with strong anonymity by routing their internet traffic through multiple relays. While Tor encrypts traffic and hides IP addresses, it remains vulnerable to traffic analysis attacks such as the website fingerprinting (WF) attack, achieving increasingly high fingerprinting accuracy even under open-world conditions. In response, researchers have proposed a variety of defenses, ranging from adaptive padding, traffic regularization, and traffic morphing to adversarial perturbation, that seek to obfuscate or reshape traffic traces. However, these defenses often entail trade-offs between privacy, usability, and system performance. Despite extensive research, a comprehensive survey unifying WF datasets, attack methodologies, and defense strategies remains absent. This paper fills that gap by systematically categorizing existing WF research into three key domains: datasets, attack models, and defense mechanisms. We provide an in-depth comparative analysis of techniques, highlight their strengths and limitations under diverse threat models, and discuss emerging challenges such as multi-tab browsing and coarse-grained traffic features. By consolidating prior work and identifying open research directions, this survey serves as a foundation for advancing stronger privacy protection in Tor.
item.dc:creator: Yuwen Cui, Guangjing Wang, Khanh Vu, Kai Wei, Kehan Shen, Zhengyuan Jiang, Xiao Han, Ning Wang, Zhuo Lu, Yao Liu

item.title: Single-Shuffle Full-Open Card-Based Secure Computation Protocols for Any Function
item.description: arXiv:2510.17308v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A card-based secure computation protocol is a method for $n$ parties to compute a function $f$ on their private inputs $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ using physical playing cards, in such a way that the suits of revealed cards leak no information beyond the value of $f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. A \textit{single-shuffle full-open} protocol is a minimal model of card-based secure computation in which, after the parties place face-down cards representing their inputs, a single shuffle operation is performed and then all cards are opened to derive the output. Despite the simplicity of this model, the class of functions known to admit single-shuffle full-open protocols has been limited to a few small examples. In this work, we prove for the first time that every function admits a single-shuffle full-open protocol. We present two constructions that offer a trade-off between the number of cards and the complexity of the shuffle operation. These feasibility results are derived from a novel connection between single-shuffle full-open protocols and a cryptographic primitive known as \textit{Private Simultaneous Messages} protocols, which has rarely been studied in the context of card-based cryptography. We also present variants of single-shuffle protocols in which only a subset of cards are revealed. These protocols reduce the complexity of the shuffle operation compared to existing protocols in the same setting.
item.dc:creator: Reo Eriguchi, Kazumasa Shinagawa

item.title: RPP: A Certified Poisoned-Sample Detection Framework for Backdoor Attacks under Dataset Imbalance
item.description: arXiv:2602.00183v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep neural networks are highly susceptible to backdoor attacks, yet most defense methods to date rely on balanced data, overlooking the pervasive class imbalance in real-world scenarios that can amplify backdoor threats. This paper presents the first in-depth investigation of how the dataset imbalance amplifies backdoor vulnerability, showing that (i) the imbalance induces a majority-class bias that increases susceptibility and (ii) conventional defenses degrade significantly as the imbalance grows. To address this, we propose Randomized Probability Perturbation (RPP), a certified poisoned-sample detection framework that operates in a black-box setting using only model output probabilities. For any inspected sample, RPP determines whether the input has been backdoor-manipulated, while offering provable within-domain detectability guarantees and a probabilistic upper bound on the false positive rate. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, TinyImageNet and ImageNet10) covering 10 backdoor attacks and 12 baseline defenses show that RPP achieves significantly higher detection accuracy than state-of-the-art defenses, particularly under dataset imbalance. RPP establishes a theoretical and practical foundation for defending against backdoor attacks in real-world environments with imbalanced data.
item.dc:creator: Miao Lin, Feng Yu, Rui Ning, Lusi Li, Jiawei Chen, Qian Lou, Mengxin Zheng, Chunsheng Xin, Hongyi Wu

item.title: TENNOR: Trustworthy Execution for Neural Networks through Obliviousness and Retrievals
item.description: arXiv:2605.07160v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training neural networks on sensitive data in untrusted cloud environments requires simultaneously achieving computational efficiency and rigorous privacy guarantees. Sparsification techniques, essential for scalable training of wide layers, expose input-dependent memory-access patterns that are visible and can be exploited by a host OS/hypervisor, even when computation is protected by a Trusted Execution Environment. We present TENNOR, a system that resolves this tension by co-designing the neural network training pipeline with doubly oblivious primitives, eliminating value-dependent neural network access-pattern leakage while also utilizing adaptive sparsification. TENNOR recasts sparse neuron activation as a locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) retrieval problem, reducing secure sparsification to doubly oblivious accesses over an LSH data structure. To eliminate the prohibitive storage cost of "multi-table" LSH, we introduce Multi-Probe Winner-Take-All (MP-WTA): the first multi-probe scheme for rank-based LSH, achieving a $50\times$ reduction in (hash table) memory while preserving model accuracy. We evaluate TENNOR on multi-label classification benchmarks, with output layers of up to hundreds of thousands of neurons under different batch sizes inside an Intel TDX Trusted Domain, achieving per-batch training speedups of $13\times$-$470\times$ over a Path ORAM baseline and reducing a 208-hour run to about 26 minutes.

item.title: Beyond Edge Coverage: Per-Task Data-Flow Extraction at Kernel Function Boundaries via LLVM
item.description: arXiv:2606.00455v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coverage-guided kernel fuzzers such as syzkaller rely on edge coverage trace-pc as their sole feedback signal. This context-blind approach cannot distinguish execution paths that differ only in argument values. For example, two invocations of copy_from_user() with different size parameters hit identical basic blocks yet have vastly different security implications. I present, an LLVM-based instrumentation framework that extends Linux KCOV with data-flow extraction of function arguments and return values. A compiler pass emits lightweight callbacks that report one source-level parameter per call, passing the value itself in a register together with its index and byte size. A composite is instead reported by the address of the object holding it, paired with a constant table of field (offset, size) pairs derived from DWARF DICompositeType metadata, with zero source annotation. The callbacks carry no program counter. The kernel derives it from the return address, which also attributes records the compiler emitted from inside an inlined body to the callee that was inlined. A lock-free per-task record buffer delivers variable-length records to user space with no interference to existing KCOV or syzkaller infrastructure, carrying entry, return, and comparison-operand records in one unified stream. I demonstrate dual utility: (1) fuzzers gain state-aware feedback for mutation guidance into value-dependent state transitions, and (2) security analysts obtain deterministic argument records for root-cause analysis without printk or kprobe overhead.

item.title: Privacy-Preserving Intent Fulfilment and Assurance for 6G RAN
item.description: arXiv:2607.08809v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Intent-based network management automates 6G service lifecycles, but existing fulfilment and assurance approaches require traffic inspection, per-flow tracking, or vendor-internal telemetry. These requirements conflict with privacy constraints in multi-tenant networks and vendor opacity in O-RAN deployments. We present an architecture that provisions resources from declared intent categories without traffic inspection and verifies fulfilment using only cell-level standardised PM counters at the O1 interface. A data-processing inequality bounds resource-allocation leakage about traffic content by $\log_2 K$ bits for $K$ categories. Intent-traffic unlinkability and node-opaque verification hold by construction. If verification requires at least $q$ cells per category among $M$ cells, the ceiling becomes $\log_2 \lfloor M/q \rfloor$ bits. This bound covers the category/resource channel, not total inference from PM counters. When individual records add state-independent noise to the category aggregate, the category-mean verifier is at least as powerful as any per-agent verifier. We map the architecture to the 3GPP intent lifecycle and O-RAN Non-RT RIC. On production PM data from four operator networks, the category-mean score has higher AUC on three networks and comparable AUC on the fourth under category-wide replacement, while per-cell screening suits sparse faults. These injection-based experiments do not establish the theorem's observation premise. Within-period cell co-movement limits a category mean to the evidence of 6 to 14 independent cells, and category-level verifiers need per-category calibration.
